\chapter{Naming Who Someone Is}
\label{ch:ka-roles}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone's role is in Kannada --- teacher, student, doctor, farmer, guest --- and name the root that two of those words share.}

Complete KA-C48-guest and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[śikṣaka]{\kn{ಶಿಕ್ಷಕ} (śikṣaka) — a teacher}

\label{lesson:KA-C48-teacher}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{hoṭṭe} mean, and what did \emph{beraḷu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಶಿಕ್ಷಕ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಶಿಕ್ಷಕ}} (\emph{śikṣaka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{śikṣaka}, 'one who teaches', on a root that covers learning and training alike; the same root gives \kn{ಶಿಕ್ಷಣ} (\emph{śikṣaṇa}), education.

The formal word is not what a Kannada child shouts across a classroom. That is \kn{ಮೇಷ್ಟ್ರು} (\emph{mēṣṭru}), which is the English \emph{master} worn smooth by a century of Kannada mouths — a schoolroom loan that arrived with the schoolroom.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five ways to say who someone is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śikṣaka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śikṣaka}, then ask \emph{nimma hesaru ēnu?} as though meeting one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಶಿಕ್ಷಕ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vidyārthi]{\kn{ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ} (vidyārthi) — a student}

\label{lesson:KA-C48-student}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{śikṣaka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ}} (\emph{vidyārthi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.

Two Sanskrit pieces: \emph{vidyā}, knowledge, and \emph{arthin}, one who seeks a thing. A student is a knowledge-seeker, said straight out.

\emph{vidyā} rests on a root meaning 'to know', and that root is among the oldest things in this book. It is the \emph{wit} of English, the \emph{vidēre} of Latin, and the first syllable of \emph{vision}. A word for a schoolchild in Bengaluru and a word for eyesight in Rome are one word with three thousand years between them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a teacher and a student.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vidyārthi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śikṣaka}, then \emph{vidyārthi}, and say which of the two is doing the seeking
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaidya]{\kn{ವೈದ್ಯ} (vaidya) — a doctor}

\label{lesson:KA-C48-doctor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vidyārthi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ವೈದ್ಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ವೈದ್ಯ}} (\emph{vaidya}) — \textquotedblleft{}a doctor\textquotedblright{}.

Here is the seeker's root a second time. \emph{vaidya} is built directly on \emph{vidyā}: 'one versed in the knowledge'. Which knowledge is left unsaid, because for the people who coined the word there was only one worth naming that way — the knowledge of medicine.

So the student and the doctor are the same word twice over, once for the one still looking and once for the one who has found. \kn{ವೈದ್ಯ} carries the older physician of the herb-books with it; the doctor at the clinic is more often \kn{ಡಾಕ್ಟರ್}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and two of the three are the same root wearing different clothes.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaidya}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vidyārthi}, then \emph{vaidya}, and hear \emph{vid-} survive in both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ವೈದ್ಯ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a doctor\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raita]{\kn{ರೈತ} (raita) — a farmer}

\label{lesson:KA-C48-farmer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vaidya} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ರೈತ}}
\textbf{\kn{ರೈತ}} (\emph{raita}) — \textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ರೈತ} came the long way round. Arabic \emph{raʿīyat}, 'the flock, the governed people', travelled through Persian into the administrative language of the Deccan and came out the other side as the word for the man who works the land and pays the revenue on it. English took the same word from the same offices and spelled it \emph{ryot}.

Kannada has an older and homelier word beside it — \kn{ಒಕ್ಕಲಿಗ} (\emph{okkaliga}), from \emph{okkalu}, a household that farms — but \kn{ರೈತ} is what a newspaper prints.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. A teacher, a student, a doctor, a farmer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raita}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all four, and say which one did not come from Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ರೈತ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[atithi]{\kn{ಅತಿಥಿ} (atithi) — a guest}

\label{lesson:KA-C48-guest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{raita} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಅತಿಥಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅತಿಥಿ}} (\emph{atithi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{atithi}, and the traditional reading of it is \emph{a-tithi}: 'one without a date'. A guest, on that reading, is exactly the person who sent no word ahead — who arrives on no appointed day and must be fed regardless. The old formula \emph{atithi devo bhava}, 'let the guest be as a god to you', is built on that idea and has outlived the grammar that produced it.

Five ways to say who someone is. Four came from Sanskrit, one from Arabic by way of Persian, and two of the four Sanskrit ones are the same root twice.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five roles: a teacher, a student, a doctor, a farmer, a guest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{atithi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then name the two that share a root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಅತಿಥಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
